purpose: Resolve the historical Guinayangan Capuluan Reef/Palad Reef name conflict using a later Ragay Gulf study and current official nautical reference. This is not a reef survey, legal boundary validation, finfish inventory, or navigation advice.
searchMethod: Bounded public-web retrieval on 2026-11-01 of the full 2022 open-access article, official 2025 NGA Pub. 162 (corrected through 2026-03-07), the 2004 CRMP directory, legacy Guinayangan tourism page, and PSA PSGC barangay listing. This source crosswalk does not establish a complete geographic or legal record.

sourcesReviewed.citation: Gordula, R. P., Lampos Jr., F. B., & Favor, C. C. (2022). Socio-Economic Assessment of the Slipper Lobster (Thenus orientalis, Lund, 1793) fishery in Ragay Gulf. Journal of Ecosystem Science and Eco-Governance, 4(Special Issue), 33-37. https://doi.org/10.54610/jeseg/4.Special_Issue.2022.004
sourcesReviewed.reviewedLocation: Printed pages 33-37; study-area text at p.34.
sourcesReviewed.result: The article describes four Ragay Gulf reef localities: Acha between Guinayangan and Tagkawayan; Kapuluan between Guinayangan and Buenavista; Palad between San Narciso and San Andres; and Ugtok southwest of Ragay, Camarines Sur. Its study lasted November 2017-October 2018 and used purposive interviews of 120 slipper-lobster fishers across four towns/gears. The article states these reefs were areas where fishers captured slipper lobsters, but reports no finfish taxa or site-resolved biological sample list. Printed p.33 identifies a Creative Commons Attribution license; version not independently verified.
sourcesReviewed.decision: Strong source evidence that the study treats Kapuluan and Palad as separate named places. Historical lobster fishery locality context only; no finfish presence, abundance, boundary, current conditions, or fishing advice.

sourcesReviewed.citation: National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. 2025. Pub. 162, Sailing Directions (Enroute): Philippine Islands. 14th ed., corrected through 7 March 2026.
sourcesReviewed.reviewedLocation: Printed p.71 for Palad Reef; printed p.72 for Capuluan Reef and Guinayangan; front matter p.ii for publication statement.
sourcesReviewed.result: The official publication separately describes Palad Reef at 13°27′N, 122°42′E, 4.75 nautical miles north of Alibijaban Island and extending about 2 miles NNW; it separately describes Capuluan Reef at 13°49′N, 122°34′E, about 2 miles east of Capuluan Point. It identifies Guinayangan town separately near Capuluan Point. Front matter says no copyright is claimed under Title 17 U.S.C. and notes correction through 7 March 2026.
sourcesReviewed.decision: Independent official navigational description distinguishes the reef names and their locations. Coordinates are recorded only to explain the identity decision; they are not imported as Bangwit geometry or a Philippine legal boundary.

sourcesReviewed.citation: Coastal Resource Management Project of DENR and USAID. 2004. Directory of CRM Learning Destinations in the Philippines.
sourcesReviewed.result: The directory entry names Nabangka Fish Sanctuary at Capuluan Central and states Capuluan Reef is also known as Palad Reef. It describes itself as a quick guide from entries submitted by LGUs.
sourcesReviewed.decision: Retain its Reef equivalence only as a historical name claim; later 2022 and 2025 sources independently distinguish the features. Its separate Nabangka locality remains unchanged.

sourcesReviewed.citation: Municipality of Guinayangan. Legacy tourism page, Natures Wonder / Palad Reef.
sourcesReviewed.result: The page places Palad Reef at Barangay Capuluan Central, describes coral and aquarium fishes generically, and says it was proposed as another sanctuary.
sourcesReviewed.decision: This is a contradictory legacy locality claim, not a finfish survey or evidence that a sanctuary was declared. Do not merge Palad with Capuluan Reef.

sourcesReviewed.citation: Philippine Statistics Authority. Guinayangan, Quezon PSGC barangay listing as of 31 July 2025.
sourcesReviewed.result: Capuluan Central is listed as barangay code 0405618011.
sourcesReviewed.decision: Administrative name and code check only; it does not resolve the Palad Reef locality claim or delineate a marine feature.

siteCrosswalk.outcome: Capuluan Reef is retained as the canonical source-backed lead from the 2004 directory and 2025 NGA description. The 2022 study spells Kapuluan and gives nearby intermunicipal context; the spelling/feature crosswalk is plausible but not normalized as a formal alias. The historical Capuluan Reef/Palad Reef equivalence is rejected.

Palad Reef is retained as a separate Ragay Gulf research lead. The study places it between San Narciso and San Andres; NGA describes it near Alibijaban Island, separately from Capuluan Reef. Neither source supplies a legal boundary or a validated geometry.
Nabangka remains a separate historical sanctuary name at Capuluan Central; the full ordinance, current status, legal boundary, and fish survey remain unverified.
The 2022 article adds historical gulf-wide lobster-fishery interview context only; it does not resolve the 13 old vernacular finfish labels or assign any finfish label to a reef.

geometryAndLegalStatus.note: No source provides a Philippine legal technical description for these reef leads. NGA coordinates are navigation-reference evidence only and are not app geometry.

limitations: The 2004 CRMP directory and municipal tourism page are historical and contain locality claims contradicted by later sources.
The 2022 study concerns slipper-lobster fishery interviews, not finfish sampling; no reef-specific finfish taxa are reported.
The 2025 NGA publication is a navigational reference, not a Philippine cadastre, reef survey, or safety/permission source.
The exact normalization of study spelling Kapuluan to NGA/CRMP spelling Capuluan is not formalized as an alias.
No legal sanctuary boundary, current sanctuary status, finfish species list, current presence/absence, catchability, diet, safety, or public-app data is established.
nextAction: Continue the Guinayangan source queue with a primary freshwater fish-survey retrieval or an official reef/fish-sanctuary document. Keep Nabangka, Capuluan Reef, and Palad Reef separate; seek dated station-resolved finfish evidence and rights review without waiting for the municipal-water inquiry.
